OpenVLA.narr: VLAs are huge — billions of parameters — so deploying them on real robots is slow. This work asks: can we keep the pretrained backbone and fine-tune it cheaply? The answer is adapter layers: frozen LLM weights with trainable lightweight adapters injected at key points. On 970k demonstrations across tasks and robots, efficient fine-tuning wins: one open model, all the generalization, a fraction of the cost.
OpenVLA.how:
The mechanism: Start with a 7B pretrained VLM frozen solid. Inject learnable adapter modules — typically linear projections or bottleneck layers — at attention heads and feed-forward blocks. During fine-tuning, only these adapters move; the backbone stays locked. This cuts the tuned parameters from billions to millions while preserving the web knowledge.

Why it works: The pretrained backbone already understands vision and language. Adapters learn the thin film of task-specific alignment — how to read the observation for this robot's morphology and what action tokens mean in this context. The backbone's prior is strong enough that adapters alone suffice, so you avoid catastrophic forgetting and can deploy on modest hardware.

Octo.narr: Most VLAs are trained on a single dataset. This work collects and unifies the Open X-Embodiment dataset: 800k trajectories from 22 different robot morphologies (arms, legs, wheeled bases). A single transformer policy learns to handle them all, conditioned on either language instructions or goal images. This is the generalist backbone that appears in diffusion-policy papers and becomes industry-standard.
Octo.how:
The mechanism: Take a transformer encoder-decoder. Input: a stack of 6 image frames + action history + language instruction or goal image. Output: 8 action dimensions, predicted autoregressively. The key innovation is the robot-agnostic action space: normalize each robot's actions into a common range (e.g., joint-space with gripper), so the model sees actions from a humanoid, a quadruped, and a mobile manipulator as points in the same learned manifold.

Why it works: By training on such diverse embodiments, the model learns what generalizes: semantic understanding of the scene (from web pretraining) and kinematic principles (from the mix). Deploy on a new robot with a few hundred demos, and it learns rapidly because the backbone already grasps the common structure.

Scaling Cross-Embodied Learning.narr: Training on one robot teaches one morphology. Can you scale to many? This paper takes 900k trajectories from arms, quadrupeds, wheeled robots, and aerial vehicles, pooling them into one dataset. A single policy emerges that generalizes to any of them — sometimes zero-shot, always with less data than a specialist would need. The key: shared representations of action and perception at the right abstraction level.
Scaling Cross-Embodied Learning.how:
The mechanism: Represent observations (images, proprioception) and actions in a robot-agnostic latent space. For images, use a pretrained vision backbone; for actions, normalize by morphology-specific scaling. Train a single policy network on the mixed data, and during inference, condition on task instructions and robot identity (or infer it from the proprioceptive signal). The policy learns generalizable primitives (reach, grasp, move) that apply across embodiments.

Why it works: When the representation layer handles the morphology translation, the policy learns task-level semantics that transfer. A 'reach' means something across all robots even though joint angles differ; the representation layer maps that semantic primitive to each body's kinematics.

A3VLM.narr: Saying 'open it' to a robot is useless unless the robot knows this object is a hinged door, where the hinge axis is, and how to grip the handle. A3VLM (articulation-aware VLM) predicts not just object identity but articulation structure: this part is the handle, this axis rotates, this rotates up to 90 degrees. That prediction transfers to new doors the robot never saw, because the geometric reasoning about articulation is object-general.
A3VLM.how: The problem: 'Open it' requires understanding part geometry and constraints, not just object type. The mechanism: Given an image of an object and an instruction, the VLM predicts a structured affordance: which part is the handle (bounding box), where is the hinge axis (line in 3D), what is the motion primitive (rotate, slide, pull). Convert these into constraints for motion planning. Why it works: Articulation structure is shared across instances (all hinges rotate around an axis), so predicting structure instead of memorizing per-object behavior generalizes to unseen objects.

Harmon.narr: Humanoid robots move like humans, so human motion priors are powerful. This work takes human motion capture data — whole-body motion sequences — and uses language descriptions to align them with instructions. The pretrained VLM learns to refine and ground those human priors into robot commands. The result: a humanoid policy that moves naturally and generalizes to new tasks faster because it inherits human kinematic structure.
Harmon.how:
The mechanism: Collect mocap sequences of humans performing tasks (reach, pick, place) and annotate each with language descriptions ('pick up the mug', 'move to the left'). Use a VLM to encode the language and the mocap (as joint sequences). Train the model to predict the next human pose given the instruction and context. Adapt this to robot kinematics by learning a morphology-aware projection from mocap space to robot joint space.

Why it works: Human motion is a strong prior for humanoid form factors; mocap data is abundant; language descriptions are cheap to collect. By anchoring robot learning to human motion, the policy inherits natural, efficient movements. The VLM's language grounding ensures the human priors are correctly applied to the instruction.

MM-ACT.narr: VLAs emit text, but robots need simultaneous outputs: language reasoning, images (for visualization), and action tokens, all in one go. This paper unifies them: a single transformer predicts text, image patches, and action tokens in parallel at 40Hz. The multimodal output lets the model reason (in language), show its thinking (in images), and act — all coherently without sequential bottlenecks.
MM-ACT.how:
The mechanism: Extend the transformer's output head to emit three token streams in parallel. Discretize actions into K bins per dimension (e.g., 256 bins for each joint), images into patch tokens (like VQVAE), and language as usual. During training, minimize cross-entropy on all three streams jointly. At inference, sample from the action distribution autoregressively but grab the language and image tokens in parallel.

Why it works: Parallel decoding is faster than sequential — no latency pipeline. Unifying modalities in one model lets the policy align reasoning and action implicitly; the transformer's self-attention mechanism keeps them consistent. The learned action tokens are now part of a rich representation that also captures language semantics and visual reasoning.

Motus.narr: Robot data is scarce but internet video is abundant. Yet video has no action labels. This work learns a latent action space from unlabeled video by watching how things move (optical flow). A VLA pretrained on that latent space then fine-tunes on scarce robot data and already understands many behaviors. Internet scale meets robot precision.
Motus.how:
The mechanism: (1) Extract optical flow from unlabeled video sequences. (2) Train an autoencoder to compress flow into a compact latent action code z. (3) Pretrain a VLA to predict z from images and language on huge video corpora. (4) Fine-tune the decoder z → robot actions on small robot datasets. The VLA learns rich motion semantics from video, then adapts the final layer to robot kinematics.

Why it works: The latent space captures general dynamics — 'reach toward', 'rotate', 'grasp' — learned from millions of videos. That's a powerful prior. Fine-tuning only the action decoder means robot data only needs to teach the morphology-specific translation, not the whole policy. Pretraining on latent actions from video is much more data-efficient than random initialization.

WAM-Flow.narr: Action tokenization is simple but autoregressive prediction is slow — one token per step. Diffusion and flow matching can sample entire action trajectories in parallel. This paper applies discrete flow matching to action tokens: generate all action tokens at once, not sequentially, three times faster than autoregressive while staying multimodal and sample-diverse.
WAM-Flow.how:
The mechanism: Model the action sequence as a flow — a straight path in latent space from noise to data. The flow-matching model learns to predict the velocity field along that path. At inference, start with noise and follow the velocity field (with ODE solver or learned step function) to generate the full sequence in parallel. Discretize the continuous trajectory into action tokens post-hoc.

Why it works: Parallel generation is fast; flow matching converges faster than diffusion because it skips the noise-to-data detour. Since all action dimensions are generated jointly (not autoregressively), they're implicitly correlated — the trajectory is naturally smooth. Multimodality emerges from sample diversity in the noise; the model learns the conditional distribution, not a point estimate.

Equivariant Diffusion Policy.narr: A diffusion head on a VLA is general but can ignore symmetry — rotating an object 90 degrees shouldn't require relearning the grasp. This paper bakes equivariance into the diffusion process: the noise schedule, the denoise steps, and the action output respect rotations and reflections. More data-efficient, more reliable to perturbations.
Equivariant Diffusion Policy.how:
The mechanism: Parameterize actions as SE(3) transformations (position + rotation) or their local frames. Build the diffusion model to respect group symmetries: noise is applied equivariantly, the denoiser network uses equivariant layers (e.g., via Lie algebra or steerable CNNs), and the output is an equivariant action. During training, the diffusion loss is symmetric under the group.

Why it works: When the model respects symmetry, it learns less and generalizes more. A grasp trained on one orientation automatically works at others (up to the gripper's constraints). This cuts the data needed to cover pose space and improves reliability to viewpoint changes, which is common in real deployment where cameras shift.

Trust the PRoC3S.narr: Making coffee needs many steps: boil water, grind beans, brew, pour. A flat VLA struggles with long horizons. This paper uses an LLM as a high-level planner: it emits parameterized skill code (e.g., 'Grasp(obj=mug, type=handle)'), and a constraint solver makes sure each step is kinematically feasible. Language plans the high level, solvers guarantee low-level realizability.
Trust the PRoC3S.how:
The mechanism: Give the task instruction to a language model. It outputs pseudocode: a sequence of high-level skills with parameters (e.g., grasp_pos, target_pose). For each step, a symbolic constraint solver (e.g., inverse kinematics, collision checking) verifies feasibility and computes the robot's joint solution. If a step is infeasible (unreachable), the planner backtracks and tries a different decomposition.

Why it works: LLMs excel at semantic decomposition; solvers excel at geometry and physics. By splitting the labor, each stage works with its strength. The planner doesn't need to learn to compute IK; the solver doesn't need to understand language. Sequential planning also makes debugging transparent: you can see and audit each step.

AutoGPT+P.narr: Planning fails when objects are missing or the world is incomplete. An LLM can reason about affordances ('I need the mug, which is usually in the cabinet'), but it can't act on pure reasoning. This work combines LLM affordance mapping ('if mug is needed, look in cabinet') with symbolic planning, letting the planner request missing information and adapt as the world unfolds.
AutoGPT+P.how:
The mechanism: (1) LLM produces a task plan with affordance annotations (e.g., 'grasp(mug, cabinet)' where cabinet is the assumed location). (2) Symbolic planner tries to execute it. (3) If a precondition fails (cabinet empty), the planner queries the LLM for a fallback. (4) The LLM revises the plan using domain knowledge (object locations, alternative approaches). (5) Repeat until execution succeeds or a human intervention is needed.

Why it works: The LLM's common sense handles incomplete information; the planner's verification catches infeasibility early. Interaction between them closes the loop: planning reveals gaps, the LLM fills them, planning re-verifies. This is more reliable than a single-pass LLM plan or a planner with no world knowledge.

Language-Augmented Symbolic Planner.narr: Symbolic planners need accurate domain models (PDDL predicates), which are hand-authored and brittle. This paper uses LLM error diagnosis to grow the domain: when a plan fails, ask the LLM why, use its explanation to add or refine predicates, and re-plan. Over time, the planner's world model becomes richer and more accurate without manual annotation.
Language-Augmented Symbolic Planner.how:
The mechanism: (1) Start with a minimal symbolic domain (e.g., locations, objects, reachability). (2) Execute a plan. (3) If it fails (e.g., pick fails), feed the failure trace to an LLM: 'Grasp failed at mug in cabinet. Why?' (4) The LLM diagnoses: 'The mug is too far back; the gripper can't reach it.' (5) Extract that as a new predicate: reachable(gripper, obj) ∧ depth(obj) < threshold. (6) Re-plan with the richer model.

Why it works: LLMs are good at explaining failure modes; symbolic planners are good at using that information to avoid the same pitfall. This closes a knowledge-collection loop: live experience reveals gaps, language reasoning diagnoses them, and the planner internalizes the fix. Over thousands of episodes, the domain grows automatically.

INTERPRET.narr: Planning from language requires learning the task structure: which objects matter, which predicates define the state, what sequence of actions works. Instead of hand-authoring PDDL, this work learns predicates from language feedback. Tell the robot 'that's wrong, I meant the other mug' and it updates its predicate for 'mug' — the model learns to generalize task structure from corrections.
INTERPRET.how:
The mechanism: (1) A learner outputs a PDDL-like predicate for each task concept (e.g., 'target-mug' is a learned linear classifier over language embeddings and scene features). (2) Execute a plan. (3) Human corrects: 'No, this mug.' (4) Use that correction to refine the predicate: update its weights to distinguish the intended mug from the predicted one. (5) Replan and re-execute.

Why it works: By treating predicates as learnable classifiers, the model can adapt to user intent from a few corrections. Language feedback directly updates the predicate representation, so the planner learns to discriminate the right objects and states. Over a task sequence, predicates generalize: once you teach 'mug' once, it works for all mugs.

MOKA.narr: Grasping objects by name ('pick the red cup') requires finding the object and reaching toward it. But objects are never perfectly labeled — the scene is cluttered and occluded. This work uses visual prompting: the VLM marks the object (e.g., draws a circle or outputs a point), and that mark becomes a 3D grasp target. Language reason, spatial output, no task-specific training.
MOKA.how:
The mechanism: (1) User says 'pick the red cup' and the image. (2) VQA prompting: 'Where is the red cup? Mark it on the image.' (3) Model outputs a spatial coordinate (pixel or normalized). (4) Lift that 2D mark to 3D using depth. (5) Compute an approach vector and gripper orientation (e.g., toward nearest edge, aligned with vertical). (6) Grasp there. A new object with no task data works immediately.

Why it works: The VLM's object recognition is generalizable (learned on web images); spatial marking is simple and independent of object class. By decoupling recognition (VLM strength) from kinematics (geometry solver), the method generalizes to any object — mushroom, wrench, fruit — without per-object training. The mark is the interface.

Manipulate-Anything.narr: Learning manipulation from human data is hard because humans have hands; robots have grippers. But if you generate trajectories with the VLM — ask it to produce a sequence of end-effector poses for a task — and clone those trajectories (no privileged state), the robot learns without demonstrations. Generative policy directly from language.
Manipulate-Anything.how:
The mechanism: (1) Instruction: 'stack the red block on the blue block.' (2) VLM imagination: prompt it to generate a sequence of end-effector poses and gripper states (open/close) as text or latent vectors. (3) Simulate those poses (forward kinematics) and capture the trajectory. (4) Behavioral clone: train a policy to predict the next pose given the current observation and the imagined trajectory. (5) At test time, condition on new objects and the same trajectory structure generalizes.

Why it works: VLMs have learned reasonable spatial structure from internet images, so their generated trajectories are often plausible. Cloning learned trajectories beats cloning from human data because humans have different morphology and physics. The VLM is an imagination engine; behavioral cloning is the execution teacher.

Towards Open-World Grasping with Large V.narr: Open-vocabulary grasping needs to handle occlusion and clutter. Simply detecting 'the mug' fails when it's hidden behind a cup. This paper has the VLM reason about parts: which visible part of the mug can I see? Use that part to compute a grasp. Under occlusion, part-level reasoning is more reliable than object-level detection.
Towards Open-World Grasping with Large V.how:
The mechanism: (1) Scene and instruction. (2) VLM predicts part-level affordances: 'I see the handle (part of mug), the spout (part of pot), and the lid (part of container).' (3) For the requested object, find its visible parts. (4) Compute a grasp on the part (e.g., approach the handle from the side, gripper angle vertical). (5) Execute. Clutter and occlusion are handled by part selection, not re-detection.

Why it works: Parts are more reliably recognizable than whole objects under occlusion. A gripper can often reach a handle even if the mug body is hidden. Part-level reasoning decomposes the problem: VLM recognizes parts, geometry computes grasps. This is more sample-efficient than training a detector for every occlusion configuration.

RAM.narr: Grasping unseen objects is hard without task data. But you can build an affordance bank — a learned library of grasp strategies associated with object features — and retrieve the best one at test time. Train on diverse object categories; at deployment, even unseen objects match to similar strategies and transfer zero-shot.
RAM.how:
The mechanism: (1) Offline: for each training object, extract features (shape, size, texture descriptors). Collect successful grasps and label each with the object features and grasp pose. Build a learnable embedding space where objects cluster by graspability. (2) At test: extract features from a unseen object. Retrieve the nearest-neighbor grasps from the bank. (3) Adapt the grasp pose to the unseen object's geometry (e.g., scale by size difference). (4) Execute.

Why it works: Affordance banks draw on the latent structure of graspability — certain shapes are easier to grasp regardless of object identity. By learning an embedding where similar-to-grasp objects cluster, retrieval becomes effective even for unseen categories. The retrieval + adaptation two-step avoids memorization while scaling to unseen objects.

TRM-VLA.narr: Long-horizon tasks (pick → place → release) need memory and hierarchical reasoning. A flat VLA fails because it can't remember earlier steps. This paper uses hierarchical chain-of-thought: model reasons through sub-goals (tokens -77.6% reduction), triggered by visual keyframes, with memory tracking. Success on 90-task benchmarks improves +28.6%.
TRM-VLA.how:
The mechanism: (1) Encode the scene and instruction into a context. (2) Detect a keyframe trigger (e.g., gripper closed after grasp, or time elapsed). (3) At each keyframe, VLA generates a chain-of-thought: the next few sub-goals in language. (4) Use a learned memory module (e.g., attention over past observations and reasoning traces) to ground the CoT in prior states. (5) Predict the action conditioned on the CoT and memory. (6) Execute and advance the state.

Why it works: Hierarchical reasoning reduces the token burden — the model doesn't recalculate the whole plan every step, only at keyframes. Memory grounds reasoning in task progress, preventing the model from drifting into impossible sub-goals. This is much more efficient than flat autoregressive planning and more reliable than reactive policies.

OctoNav.narr: A single policy that handles object navigation ('find a mug'), point navigation ('go to this GPS coordinate'), image navigation ('reach a scene like this photo'), and language-instruction navigation all at once is far more useful than four separate models. OctoNav unifies these by training on a giant mix of all four task types with a shared backbone, using language prompts to specify which task to solve. Generalist navigation earns transfer for free.
OctoNav.how: The problem: Each navigation task needs its own model, fragmenting data and inference. The mechanism: Train a single VLA policy on concatenated data from all four navigation tasks — object nav, point nav, image nav, language nav — with a learned prompt token that tells the policy which task is active. Use action-supervised fine-tuning (Action-SFT) to imitate expert policies, then reinforcement learning (navigation GRPO) to improve. Why it works: The backbone learns shared representations for place, landmark, and spatial reasoning across task types, so competence on one task transfers to others.

HybridDriveVLA.narr: Driving safely requires predicting how the scene will evolve — other cars, pedestrians, turning vehicles — not just reacting to the current frame. HybridDriveVLA has the VLA reason through candidate trajectories using a tree-of-thought approach: generate several possible paths, predict how the scene will look if the robot follows each one (via future-frame prediction), then score each for collision risk and comfort. This trajectory-conditioned future reasoning anticipates hazards the current frame alone would miss.
HybridDriveVLA.how: The problem: Reacting to the present frame lags the world's dynamics. The mechanism: Generate a set of candidate trajectories (straight, left turn, right turn, yield, etc.). For each, use a learned world model to predict future camera frames. Score each prediction for obstacles (collisions), progress toward the goal, and ride comfort. Pick the trajectory with the best score. Why it works: Explicit future prediction surfaces potential crashes before they happen; tree-of-thought gives the model multiple hypotheses to reason over.

ACoT-VLA.narr: Actions are easier to reason about when you break them down first. Instead of predicting action tokens directly, this paper has the model emit an action chain-of-thought: reasoning about the task step, the object involved, and the motion needed, then predict the action. Intermediate reasoning improves coherence and reliability.
ACoT-VLA.how:
The mechanism: (1) Scene and instruction encoded. (2) VLA generates an action CoT: 'This is a pick task. The target is the red mug on the left. I should approach from above, open gripper, descend, close gripper.' (3) From that reasoning, extract a representation (e.g., latent vector or a next-word prediction in a reasoning language). (4) Condition the action prediction on both the scene and that reasoning trace. (5) Predict the action (joint angles, gripper state).

Why it works: Intermediate reasoning acts as a bottleneck — it forces the model to commit to a conceptual plan before committing to kinematics. If the reasoning is wrong ('open gripper' when it should be closed), the action prediction can still correct it because it's conditioned on both. This intermediate step also makes the policy's decision auditable: you can see what it decided to do and why.

SpatialBot.narr: A vision-language model excels at semantics—it names objects, understands affordances, and reasons about relationships. But ask it ‘where is the mug?’ and it points to a spot on the 2D image, not a location in real 3D space. For a robot manipulator, 5–10 centimeters of error means grasping air instead of the target. SpatialBot anchors the VLM’s semantic labels onto an explicit 3D scene graph—a structured representation of objects, surfaces, and their spatial relationships—so that language-driven goals land at the precise metric coordinates a gripper needs.
SpatialBot.how:
1. Build a 3D scene graph: from RGB-D or multi-view inputs, reconstruct the scene geometry (depth + segmentation), identify objects and planes, and encode their positions, sizes, and adjacencies as a graph structure.
  2. Map language to graph nodes: when the VLM says ‘the mug,’ ground that semantic prediction to the object node in the graph that best matches the visual and spatial context.
  3. Query metric coordinates: once the semantic label is anchored to a graph node, extract its 3D position, orientation, and contact surfaces directly from the scene geometry, not from 2D image coordinates.
  4. Why it works: by factoring perception into language (semantic understanding) and geometry (3D structure), the robot gets both the right label and the right location—centimeter-accurate reach-and-grasp is now possible.

VLM-Grounder.narr: A VLM can reason about spatial relationships in language (‘to the left of the sink,’ ‘near the back’), but translating loose spatial descriptions into precise 3D points is a two-stage problem: first identify the region of interest, then refine to the exact 3D coordinate. VLM-Grounder handles this as a coarse-to-fine agent loop—start with a broad search using language and visual features, then iteratively zoom in and query the VLM for sub-meter, then centimeter-scale precision, until the model’s uncertainty drops below the gripper’s tolerance.
VLM-Grounder.how:
1. Coarse pass: the VLM receives a linguistic query (‘find the red mug on the counter’) and the full scene image. It produces a rough bounding region or depth estimate using commonsense spatial reasoning—no explicit 3D model yet, just visual features and text.
  2. Refine iteratively: crop or zoom the region, feed it back to the VLM with a follow-up prompt asking for a more precise 3D location. Each cycle of the loop narrows the search space and reduces the model’s spatial ambiguity.
  3. Confidence and termination: track the VLM’s uncertainty (e.g., disagreement across rephrased queries or predicted confidence scores). Stop refining when the uncertainty becomes small enough—typically centimeter-scale for reach tasks.
  4. Why it works: VLMs are weak at absolute 3D estimation but strong at binary comparisons (‘is this closer or farther?’). Coarse-to-fine draws on that strength, asking the model only for relative refinements until the cumulative error is acceptable for control.

ActiveVLA.narr: Manipulation tasks require precise 3D coordination. A 2D camera image is inherently ambiguous about depth and scale—the same pixel could be 10cm away or 50cm away. ActiveVLA combines active view selection (choosing camera angles) with multi-view projection to build a 3D map of the workspace, then reasons over this precise 3D geometry to plan manipulation, reaching 91.8% success on complex benchmarks.
ActiveVLA.how:
The problem: Single-view 2D reasoning fails on tasks requiring precise depth (inserting a peg, placing an object exactly). Multi-view data resolves ambiguity but requires a policy that knows which views matter.

The mechanism: ActiveVLA learns a view-selection policy: given the task (e.g., 'insert the peg') and current observation, the policy proposes camera poses that would be informative (top-down for seeing the hole, side views for depth). From multiple views, the model projects visual features into a 3D occupancy or feature map (using learned camera poses or explicit pose estimation). The VLA reasons over this 3D map—it sees the gripper position, the hole's 3D location, and obstacles in 3D space. Action planning then operates on this 3D geometry, predicting gripper trajectories that satisfy constraints.

Why it works: Active perception + 3D reconstruction solves two problems at once: resolve ambiguity (by collecting views) and get precise geometry (by fusing them). The multi-view projection is a learned operation, so the policy can learn which views are most informative for the task. RLBench success rates at 91.8% reflect the power of reasoning over precise 3D geometry rather than noisy 2D projections.

ReKep.narr: A VLM might say 'the mug handle', but a gripper needs exact 3D coordinates to grasp. ReKep solves this by predicting relational keypoint constraints from language: 'the gripper should be close to the handle and above the table'. These constraints are expressed as spatial relationships between keypoints in 3D (detected from RGB-D images), then optimized in real time to find a feasible grasp. This bridges language semantics to metric optimization.
ReKep.how: The problem: Language says 'here' but control needs coordinates and constraints. The mechanism: A VLM reads the instruction and predicts high-level relational constraints (e.g., 'gripper above object', 'gripper close to handle'). Detect 3D keypoints in the scene (handle position, table plane, object center). Express constraints as geometric relationships between these keypoints. Solve a real-time optimization (e.g., inverse kinematics + compliance) to satisfy the constraints. Why it works: Constraints are more reliable than direct coordinate prediction; optimization naturally handles multiple competing goals.

LeLaN.narr: Following 'go to the kitchen' through a real building requires the robot to learn navigation from watching real-world video — but human video has no action labels. LeLaN solves this by having a VLM auto-label 50+ hours of uncurated in-the-wild footage with natural-language descriptions of movement and goals, turning passive video into navigation training data. This breaks the bottleneck of collecting labeled robot demonstrations.
LeLaN.how: The problem: Navigation from language needs examples of following directions, but collecting labeled human navigation video is slow. The mechanism: Take raw videos of people moving through homes. Apply a VLM to each frame sequence to automatically label what the person is doing ('walking toward the kitchen', 'looking for a mug'). Treat those labels as natural-language goals the robot should replicate. Fine-tune a navigation policy on the auto-labeled data. Why it works: The VLM captures the semantic intent of human movement without humans having to annotate by hand, so you get 50× more training data at near-zero cost.

GOAT: Go To Any Thing.narr: A mobile robot told 'find a mug' in an unfamiliar home must explore, remember what it saw, and search efficiently. GOAT builds a semantic memory that grows as the robot moves through the space, storing what objects and places it has seen. When given an open-ended goal like 'find a mug', it queries that memory map to navigate toward promising regions, updating memory as new rooms appear. This transfers across homes with continually-augmented spatial memory.
GOAT: Go To Any Thing.how: The problem: A static map is wrong in new homes, so the robot must learn as it goes. The mechanism: As the robot navigates, a VLM watches the scene and builds a topological map, labeling each place ('kitchen', 'hallway') and each object seen ('mug on counter'). Store this as a semantic graph. When asked to find a mug, query the graph for mug locations, plan a path to the most promising one, then explore from there. Each new observation updates the map. Why it works: Semantic memory grounds navigation in language — the robot knows what to look for and where to look next, without memorizing pixel-perfect geometry.

Mobility VLA.narr: Long sentences like 'go to the kitchen, find a mug, and bring it back' hide multiple steps and spatial reasoning a flat policy struggles with. Mobility VLA uses a long-context VLM to reason over a topological graph of the environment, breaking down the instruction into subgoals (reach kitchen → search for mug → return), and selecting actions on each node of the graph. This language-conditioned graph planning makes multi-step navigation tractable.
Mobility VLA.how: The problem: A long instruction requires sequential reasoning over space, but memorizing all options in one action is hard. The mechanism: First, build a topological graph of the known space (nodes = places, edges = navigable passages). For each node, store image observations and place labels. When given an instruction, a long-context VLM reads the instruction and the graph structure, generates subgoals, then at each timestep predicts which node to move toward based on remaining subgoals. Why it works: Explicit graph structure decomposes the spatial reasoning problem; the VLM can hold the whole task structure in context and make coherent multi-step decisions.

DrivePI.narr: Autonomous driving systems usually detect objects, track them, then plan — each stage loses information. DrivePI is a compact (0.5B parameter) multimodal LLM that fuses LiDAR and cameras into a unified 4D spatial representation, reasoning about the scene in language rather than through intermediate object detections. Skipping the cascade and reasoning directly over geometry and language outperforms much larger models on real driving tasks like occupancy prediction and scene QA.
DrivePI.how: The problem: Detecting → tracking → planning loses spatial coherence, and separate detectors fail on edge cases. The mechanism: Encode LiDAR points and camera images into a shared 4D spatial token representation (bird's-eye-view + temporal). Feed this to a small VLM that reasons about occupancy, risk, and action all at once in language. No intermediate object list. Why it works: Reasoning directly over geometry avoids the detection bottleneck, and language reasoning adds interpretability; the small model size makes it practical for real time.

Percept-WAM.narr: A vision-only driving model can't reason about three-dimensional space from 2D images alone, leading to crashes at unprotected turns or with occlusion. Percept-WAM augments the VLA backbone with two parallel token streams: 2D image features (for fine visual detail) and 3D bird's-eye-view (BEV) features (for metric geometry). Fusing both streams in the backbone lets the model reason about the scene in two geometries at once, becoming reliable to both visual subtlety and spatial ambiguity.
Percept-WAM.how: The problem: 2D images alone can't judge depth or spatial extent reliably. The mechanism: Encode camera images into 2D feature tokens. In parallel, encode LiDAR or depth into a BEV voxel grid, quantize it into BEV tokens. Concatenate both streams and feed to the VLM backbone. The model attends to both 2D and 3D tokens simultaneously, learning to fuse them. Why it works: The model can ground uncertain 2D cues with 3D geometry ('that shadow' + '3D free space' = safe), and vice versa; dual geometry redundancy hardens the system.

SpaceDrive.narr: VLMs excel at semantic reasoning but struggle with geometry: 'stop before the intersection' requires knowing where the intersection is in 3D, not just recognizing it visually. SpaceDrive prepends a geometric spatial encoder that explicitly extracts 3D positions of landmarks (lane edges, stop signs, pedestrians) from camera and LiDAR, grounding that geometry as tokens the VLM attends to. This geometric-semantic fusion gives the model both language reasoning and metric coordinates.
SpaceDrive.how: The problem: VLMs reason semantically but can't extract precise 3D positions for control. The mechanism: Use a neural encoder (e.g., based on depth or LiDAR) to extract 3D keypoint positions and their confidence. Represent each landmark as a spatial token (position, type, confidence). Feed these geometric tokens alongside image tokens to the VLM. The model can now say 'the stop sign is at [x, y, z]' and reason about it. Why it works: Explicit geometry gives the planner unambiguous coordinates; the VLM wraps semantic reasoning around concrete spatial tokens.

RoboEXP.narr: A robot grasping a new object for the first time doesn't know how it will respond to forces. RoboEXP explores the object interactively — pushing, rotating, lifting — while a multimodal LLM watches and builds a scene graph: this part is soft, this part is fixed, this edge is where you can grip. The LLM builds causal action-conditioned models through interaction, learning affordances by doing rather than by being told.
RoboEXP.how: The problem: Static observation doesn't reveal how an object behaves under force. The mechanism: The robot takes small exploratory actions (light pushes, rotations). After each action, a VLM observes the result and updates a scene graph with new object properties (this part moved, this stayed fixed). Build causal links: action A led to change B. After several interactions, the scene graph contains a model of the object's affordances. Why it works: Active interaction reveals hidden structure; the LLM integrates observations into an action-conditioned model that predicts what will happen next.

Reasoning Grasping via MLLM.narr: Grasping a scissors requires understanding that you grip the loops, not the blade — the semantic intent 'use this tool' must map to specific object parts and grasp poses. A multimodal LLM reasons through that intent: 'to cut, I need to grip both loops and insert paper here', converting abstract task intent into part-level and pose-level instructions that a grasp planner can execute. This layer turns language intent into executable motor commands.
Reasoning Grasping via MLLM.how: The problem: Task intent doesn't map directly to grasp poses. The mechanism: Give the LLM the instruction ('cut the paper with scissors'), an image of the object, and the gripper model. The LLM reasons through the task (cutting requires inserting paper, which requires both loops free, which means gripping here). Output part-level targets (grip loop 1 at [x,y,z], loop 2 at [x,y,z]) and pose constraints (gripper orientation must be parallel). A grasp planner then executes. Why it works: The LLM holds the causal chain: intent → parts needed → grasp poses; this decouples semantic reasoning from geometric planning.

Yell At Your Robot.narr: A robot picking up the wrong mug and continuing is useless. Yell At Your Robot gives the robot hierarchical policies: a high-level behavior (pick the object) and fine-grained correction behaviors (adjust grip, rotate, shift left). When a human says 'no, tighter grip', the policy interprets that as a correction signal, updates its behavior online, and continues the task. Language becomes a live repair channel for mid-task correction.
Yell At Your Robot.how: The problem: Policies fail silently and can't incorporate human corrections mid-task. The mechanism: Train a hierarchical policy with high-level skills (grasp, place, push) and a bank of low-level refinement actions (adjust grip force, translate hand, rotate). During deployment, listen for spoken corrections. Map corrections ('tighter', 'to the left') to refinement actions. Execute the refinement, then continue the main task from the new state. Why it works: Hierarchical structure lets the policy respond to corrections without restarting; language corrections are precise enough to guide fine adjustments.

RACER.narr: When a policy fails, the failure is often subtle — a slipped grasp, an occlusion, a physics surprise. RACER learns recovery behaviors by watching demonstrations of both failures and recoveries, annotated with natural-language explanations ('the gripper was slipping, so I increased pressure'). The LLM reads the explanation and the state, predicting what recovery to execute. This turns failure data into a recovery skill library.
RACER.how: The problem: Failure is context-dependent; a generic recovery doesn't work for all failure modes. The mechanism: Collect demonstrations of failures paired with language explanations of the failure cause. Train the LLM to read the explanation, observe the current state (visual + proprioceptive), and output a recovery action. Use imitation learning on the failure-recovery pairs. Why it works: Language explanations label failure modes semantically; the LLM learns to match current state to past failures and apply the appropriate recovery.

Sentinel.narr: Detecting task failure is hard — did the grasp succeed or is the object just hidden? Sentinel combines multiple failure detectors (a consistency checker comparing expected vs actual state, plus a VLM progress detector) and flags a failure only when both agree. This multi-detector consensus catches 18% more true failures than any single detector, reducing false alarms that interrupt the robot.
Sentinel.how: The problem: Single detectors miss failures or raise false alarms. The mechanism: Maintain a forward model that predicts what the scene should look like if the task succeeded. Compare predicted vs actual. In parallel, use a VLM to read the instruction, watch the scene, and estimate progress. Raise a failure alert only if both detectors agree (consistency broken AND progress stalled). Why it works: Independent detectors have different failure modes; combining them reduces false positives while catching real failures.

Vocal Sandbox.narr: Teaching a robot recoverable behaviors usually requires heavy supervision — hundreds of demonstrations of each failure and recovery. Vocal Sandbox learns with less data by combining three signals: spoken dialogue corrections ('move left'), keypoint annotations (show where to go), and a few video demonstrations. This multi-modal teaching signal lets the robot learn recovery behaviors with 22% less labeled data.
Vocal Sandbox.how: The problem: Recovery behaviors need lots of supervision to generalize. The mechanism: During training, provide three forms of weak supervision: (1) natural-language corrections from a human ('the gripper is too high'), (2) keypoint annotations showing the desired pose, (3) a few full demonstrations. Train a policy on all three signals jointly. Each signal provides a different constraint on what the recovery should do. Why it works: Multiple signal types are redundant — a verbal cue + a keypoint often constrain the behavior enough, so fewer full demonstrations are needed.

MIRAGE.narr: When you train a manipulation policy on robot A, it sees that robot's arm in every frame. Move to robot B with a different arm and the model fails—it's seeing a different visual input, even though the task is the same. MIRAGE solves this by erasing the source robot from its training images and painting in the target robot instead, so the policy learns the task in a robot-agnostic way. Now a policy trained on one arm transfers zero-shot to another.
MIRAGE.how:
The problem: Visual policies overfit to the appearance of the training robot—its arm shape, color, mounting point. Transfer fails because the target robot looks totally different in the image.

The mechanism: During training, MIRAGE uses image inpainting (a diffusion model or similar) to mask out the source robot's body from each demonstration frame and fills in the target robot in its place, creating synthetic training data. The VLA trains on these inpainted images instead of the originals, learning the task motion without binding to any specific arm.

Why it works: By removing the robot's identity from the visual input, the policy learns to extract task-relevant features (object positions, hand trajectory) that generalize across embodiments. A new robot sees itself in every training image, so it feels natural.

RoVi-Aug.narr: A policy trained on a humanoid robot with a specific shoulder mount and camera angle crashes when you move the camera. Policies bind tightly to the visual appearance of their training robot. RoVi-Aug augments training data by randomly varying both the robot's identity (arm color, joint structure) and the viewpoint (camera angle, zoom), teaching the model to see past the robot's shape and focus on the task itself.
RoVi-Aug.how:
The problem: Policies learn spurious correlations between visual features and actions, like 'this shoulder shape means reach up.' Changing the robot's appearance or camera angle breaks those correlations.

The mechanism: During data augmentation, RoVi-Aug applies generative augmentation to the training demonstrations: randomly render the robot's morphology (different arm segments, colors, joint angles) and vary the viewpoint (pan, tilt, zoom the camera). The same task trajectory is re-rendered from all these new perspectives and with different robot identities, creating a huge synthetic dataset.

Why it works: Seeing a task executed from many viewpoints and with many robot appearances forces the policy to learn viewpoint-invariant and robot-invariant features. Transfer to a new embodiment with a +30% improvement shows the policy learned generalizable spatial reasoning, not surface appearance.

Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI).narr: Collecting robot demonstrations is expensive—you need a robot, you need to program it or teleoperate it, you need experts. But humans already have a universal manipulation interface: their hands. UMI learns manipulation policies directly from human hand-gripper demonstrations recorded with a cheap camera and a hand-held gripper, then transfers that policy to a full robot arm without ever seeing the target robot during training.
Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI).how:
The problem: Robot policies require robot data, but collecting robot demonstrations is slow and costly. Human videos are abundant but the mapping from human hand to robot gripper is non-obvious.

The mechanism: UMI records a human wearing a simple hand-held gripper (tracked by the camera) performing a task—picking, placing, rotating an object. The gripper's 6D pose and binary grasp signal become the 'action' in those demos. A VLA then learns to map images + language to gripper pose and grasp state. At test time on a robot, inverse kinematics converts the gripper target into joint commands; the gripper signal goes straight to the end-effector.

Why it works: The gripper is a canonical interface. The policy learns the task as 'move the gripper here, then close it'—geometry and physics that transfer directly to a robot arm. Because the training robot (the human hand-gripper) is never shown to the robot at test time, the policy never overfits to a specific embodiment.

Learning a Unified Latent Action Space.narr: Different robots have different action spaces: a quadruped outputs leg joint angles, a gripper arm outputs end-effector pose, a wheeled base outputs velocity. A single VLA policy can't output all of them at once, but it can learn a shared latent action representation that captures what all robots are doing (the task level) and then convert that latent space to each robot's native commands via cycle-consistency training.
Learning a Unified Latent Action Space.how:
The problem: Robot embodiments have incompatible action spaces (joint angles, end-effector poses, velocities). A VLA that outputs text or discrete tokens needs a different decoder for each robot type, breaking generalization.

The mechanism: This approach learns an embedding space for actions: given a demo from robot A executing a task (e.g., 'grasp the cup'), encode its actions into a latent vector. In parallel, encode the same or a similar task from robot B. Use cycle-consistency loss: encode A's actions to latent, decode to B's action space, and verify B can execute it correctly. This jointly learns the latent space and the encode/decode functions for each robot.

Why it works: The latent space captures the semantic task ('move toward object, close gripper') independent of how each robot's motors express it. A VLA trained to output latent actions generalizes to new robots because it only needs to learn their decode function, not retrain the entire policy. The +20.1% improvement over OpenVLA shows shared latent space learns faster and transfers better.

SwiftVLA.narr: A 7-billion-parameter VLA takes 2-3 seconds per inference—orders of magnitude too slow for a control loop. SwiftVLA distills the large VLA into a small student model using mask-and-reconstruct training: mask random input tokens and train the student to predict what the large teacher would have predicted. The result is 18× faster and uses 12× less memory while retaining most of the accuracy.
SwiftVLA.how:
The problem: Big VLMs are slow (seconds per action) and memory-heavy (cannot run on robot onboard hardware). Real-time control needs answers in tens of milliseconds.

The mechanism: SwiftVLA uses a masking-based distillation strategy: during training, randomly mask regions of the input image. Train a small student network to predict the teacher VLA's output even with masked inputs. This forces the student to learn to infer the full task from partial information—a stronger generalization signal than standard distillation. The student outputs the same action tokens or continuous head predictions as the teacher.

Why it works: Mask-and-reconstruct is an inductive bias for reliability and efficiency. The student learns that it doesn't need full pixel fidelity to understand the task; a coarse outline of the scene suffices. The 18× speedup allows VLAs to run in the control loop of a real robot, closing the gap between 'it works in simulation' and 'it works on hardware.'

Evo-1.narr: Efficient VLAs exist but they often lose semantic alignment—the model still outputs sensible features internally but the final action head becomes brittle. Evo-1 is designed from the ground up as a lightweight VLA, keeping the full vision-language backbone compact while preserving the semantic richness that lets it generalize and be interpretable, even on edge hardware.
Evo-1.how:
The problem: Distilling a large VLA naively cuts accuracy on out-of-distribution tasks because the compact model loses the semantic understanding of objects and language that makes VLAs general. You get speed but lose generalization.

The mechanism: Evo-1 co-designs the architecture for efficiency: use a lightweight vision encoder (e.g., a small ViT) and a smaller language model, but keep the cross-modal attention layers that fuse vision and language. Train on the same co-training recipe (web + robot data) to maintain semantic grounding. The architecture is optimized for early pruning of non-task-relevant tokens and efficient matrix operations.

Why it works: Efficiency comes from the architecture, not from throwing away knowledge. Evo-1 retains the semantic alignment between visual features, language tokens, and actions, so it generalizes to new objects and phrasings. It can run on edge devices while still reasoning about open-vocabulary instructions.

Fast-ThinkAct.narr: Reasoning VLAs that emit explicit chain-of-thought (e.g., 'I see a mug on the table, it is 10cm to the left, I will reach down and grasp') are interpretable but verbose—the language decoding can be as slow as the final action prediction. Fast-ThinkAct encodes reasoning as compact latent vectors, not tokens: the model learns to compress the reasoning into a dense representation that guides action prediction without emitting language, retaining interpretability at 1/10th the latency.
Fast-ThinkAct.how:
The problem: Chain-of-thought VLAs emit readable text reasoning but autoregressive decoding of that text is slow, making the total inference latency prohibitive for real-time control.

The mechanism: Fast-ThinkAct trains a VAE-like bottleneck: the model processes the image and instruction through a VLM encoder, then produces a compact latent code (e.g., a 64-dim vector) that encodes the reasoning step (object location, task substeps). Separately, the action head is trained to condition on this latent and output the action directly. At inference, there is no autoregressive language generation—only a single latent forward pass.

Why it works: The latent vector acts as an interpretable intermediate representation. The latent dimensions are often aligned with spatial features (object position, depth) and task features (grasp type, motion direction), so interpretability is preserved. Inference is a single feedforward pass on the latent, not a loop of token generation, cutting latency by 10× and allowing reasoning VLAs to run in control loops.

ForceVLA2.narr: A robot wiping a surface or inserting a peg cannot do it by vision alone—the moment the tool touches the surface, geometry is no longer enough. You need to feel the force and adjust. ForceVLA2 augments the VLA with force and torque sensors and a mixture-of-experts layer that learns when to trust vision versus force, routing the input to specialized experts depending on whether the robot is in contact or moving freely.
ForceVLA2.how:
The problem: Vision-language policies miss closed-loop force control. Contact dynamics (friction, compliance, required insertion force) are invisible to a camera. The policy can move the arm toward the hole but cannot feel resistance and adapt.

The mechanism: ForceVLA2 concatenates force/torque sensor readings (6D) with visual and language tokens. A mixture-of-experts gating network learns to route the combined input to one of several expert heads: one expert specializes in free-space motion (trusting vision and language), another in compliant contact (blending force feedback with visual targets). The router learns when to switch based on the current force magnitude and task phase.

Why it works: Mixture-of-experts avoids a single policy trying to be two things at once. The contact expert learns to modulate force (press harder, back off, slide) while the free-space expert reasons about geometry and objects. The +48% improvement over vision-only policies on assembly tasks shows closed-loop force feedback is not a luxury—it is the difference between success and failure on contact-rich tasks.

AT-VLA.narr: Tactile sensors on a robot gripper can feel texture, temperature, and slip, giving high-bandwidth feedback during manipulation. But integrating tactile data into a VLA is tricky—tactile signals are sparse (only when in contact) and come from many locations. AT-VLA injects tactile information adaptively: during free motion, it is ignored; during contact, the model learns to weight tactile signals according to the task phase, from initial contact detection to in-hand manipulation.
AT-VLA.how:
The problem: Tactile sensors are most informative during contact but produce noise when not touching anything. A naive fusion (always include tactile tokens) dilutes the signal. A VLA needs to learn when tactile input is relevant.

The mechanism: AT-VLA adds a tactile encoder that processes readings from fingertip sensors (pressure, shear, temperature). An attention gate learns to weight the tactile tokens: zero weight during free motion, higher weight once force is detected. The gating function is learned end-to-end; the VLA learns that slip detection (high shear relative to applied force) is important for stable grasps but heat is less informative. Tactile embedding is fused with visual tokens via cross-attention.

Why it works: Adaptive injection respects the signal-to-noise ratio of tactile data. The model learns task-specific tactile semantics (slip means adjust grip, certain textures mean slippery object). This closed-loop multimodal fusion is what makes dexterous manipulation work—you cannot see a slip, but you can feel it.

3D-ViTac.narr: A unified representation of vision and touch is powerful: the same feature space encodes both what you see and what you feel. 3D-ViTac builds a joint 3D visuo-tactile representation by fusing visual observations and tactile readings into a shared occupancy or feature grid, where both modalities contribute to the same spatial map. A VLA reasoning over this fused map beats vision-only on fragile items that need gentle handling.
3D-ViTac.how:
The problem: Vision and touch operate on different scales and modalities. Tactile sensors are sparse and local; cameras are global but cannot feel. Naive concatenation of features loses the spatial coherence that makes them useful for planning.

The mechanism: 3D-ViTac projects both visual features and tactile features into a shared 3D occupancy or voxel grid in the robot's egocentric frame. Visual features come from a ViT backbone applied to camera images; tactile features come from fingertip sensor embeddings, localized to the 3D positions of the gripper fingers. The fusion is geometric: tactile reads at (gripper_x, gripper_y, gripper_z) and updates local grid cells; visual updates global cells. The VLA reasons over this unified 3D representation to predict grasp and manipulation actions.

Why it works: Shared 3D geometry is the right abstraction. Touch tells you 'here, in 3D, the object is soft/slippery/hard'; vision tells you 'here, that object looks fragile.' The unified grid allows the policy to learn that certain grasp geometries (approaching along a certain axis) combined with tactile feedback (gentleness) leads to success on fragile items. Vision-only policies lack this feedback loop.

AVA-VLA.narr: Manipulation often requires looking around occlusions: you cannot see behind the box, so you have to move to a better angle. Fixed-camera policies fail. AVA-VLA treats this as a POMDP (partially observable Markov decision process) where the policy maintains a latent belief state across multiple views, learns to query informative views by adjusting the camera, and updates its understanding of the scene incrementally.
AVA-VLA.how:
The problem: A single camera angle is often ambiguous: is the object behind the box, or does it not exist? A fixed-camera policy commits to the first hypothesis and fails. Dynamic viewpoint selection adds degrees of freedom but requires reasoning over multiple observations.

The mechanism: AVA-VLA uses a recurrent state (e.g., a transformer hidden state or a latent embedding) that accumulates information across multiple observations. At each step, the policy observes the scene from the current camera angle, updates its state, and decides whether to act or to move the camera. The action includes a camera movement command ('pan left', 'zoom', 'rotate'). Visual tokens are dynamically reweighted by the policy based on task history: if 'grasp the mug' is the goal and you see a mug-like shape, those tokens get high weight; irrelevant clutter gets low weight. The recurrent state lets the policy remember that it already checked one location and should look elsewhere.

Why it works: POMDP reasoning models uncertainty. The policy learns that some situations require additional views before committing to an action. Dynamic visual-token reweighting by task history is a learned attention mechanism: high-value regions (likely target location given the goal) get more computation. This beats fixed-camera policies because the policy can resolve ambiguities by moving.

EgoRoC.narr: Egocentric (first-person) video from a wrist camera is the natural view for a robot arm, but it is often misaligned with the actions the robot actually takes—small shifts in camera mounting change all the pixel coordinates. EgoRoC learns hand-eye calibration end-to-end using a diffusion model: the model is trained to generate the expected next egocentric frame given the current frame and a proposed action, and mismatch between the generated and observed frames is used to refine the action.
EgoRoC.how:
The problem: Wrist-mounted cameras have inherent calibration uncertainty. The camera's pose relative to the gripper is never perfectly known, and even small misalignment breaks pixel-level action prediction.

The mechanism: EgoRoC trains a diffusion model to predict future egocentric frames: given the current frame and a candidate action (gripper position/orientation), the diffusion model denoises a distribution over possible next frames. During training, the ground-truth next frame is available. At test time, the model generates multiple candidate next frames for different actions; the action whose predicted frame best matches the observed reality (according to a learned discriminator or reconstruction loss) is selected. This is a learned inverse model: the calibration is learned implicitly because the model that predicts frames most accurately is the one with the correct hand-eye relationship.

Why it works: Diffusion models naturally represent uncertainty and can learn complex visual dynamics. The key insight is that the correct hand-eye calibration is the one under which egocentric video predictions are most accurate. By training to predict future frames without explicit pose labels, the model learns calibration as a side effect. This is task-agnostic—it works for any robot and camera configuration.

LIBERO-Plus.narr: VLAs that score 95% on clean benchmarks often collapse to <30% when the camera shifts, the lighting changes, or the user rephrases the instruction. LIBERO-Plus is a 7-dimensional perturbation benchmark that stress-tests VLAs with realistic shifts in viewpoint, lighting, layout, and language phrasing, revealing that reliability is not automatic and requires explicit hardening.
LIBERO-Plus.how:
The problem: Standard benchmarks (LIBERO, RLBench) use fixed camera angles and lighting. Real deployments face shifted cameras, dimmer light, and users saying 'pick up that blue thing' instead of 'pick up the blue cube.' Performance cliffs are hidden until deployment.

The mechanism: LIBERO-Plus systematically varies seven dimensions across evaluation: (1) camera viewpoint (pan, tilt, roll), (2) camera distance (near/far), (3) lighting brightness, (4) background clutter, (5) object scale, (6) instruction phrasing, (7) object-scene layout. For each task, dozens of variants are generated. A VLA is evaluated not just on the canonical version but on all perturbations, revealing which dimensions cause performance to drop.

Why it works: Systematic stress-testing exposes brittleness. Results show performance often crashes from 95% to <30% under modest shifts. This diagnostic accelerates progress: developers can see whether their VLA is learning reliable features (invariant to viewpoint, lighting) or overfitting to artifacts. It converts VLA reliability from a vague goal to a measurable, reproducible phenomenon.

SRPO.narr: Reliability requires not just better data but better training. SRPO (Sim-to-Real Policy Optimization) uses dense rewards from a learned world model to post-train a VLA with reinforcement learning, taking a VLA from 48.9% to 99.2% success on LIBERO in 200 RL steps, without retraining from scratch.
SRPO.how:
The problem: Supervised learning on demonstrations reaches a ceiling; data diversity is limited, and a policy that works on training tasks fails on perturbations. Reinforcement learning could fix this but requires expensive online rollouts or a good simulator.

The mechanism: SRPO learns a latent world model (e.g., a small diffusion model or VAE) that predicts the next observation given the current observation and action. This world model is learned from the existing demonstration data. Then, SRPO uses this learned world model as a reward function: the model generates predictions for multiple candidate actions, and the action whose predicted outcome is closest to the language-described goal is preferred. This is reward from a learned latent, not from pixels. RL (e.g., PPO) optimizes the VLA policy against these learned rewards in the latent world-model loop.

Why it works: Learning rewards from a world model is much cheaper than online RL with a real robot. The world model learned from demos captures task-relevant dynamics. RL on these learned rewards rapidly improves performance on the original benchmark and, critically, on perturbed versions of it. The jump from 48.9% to 99.2% shows RL closes the sim-to-real gap by learning reliable policies that the demonstration-only baseline missed.

FlowHijack.narr: Flow-matching VLAs are fast and dexterous, but are they secure? FlowHijack is the first demonstrated backdoor attack on flow-matching VLAs: by poisoning a small fraction of training data with subtle perturbations, an attacker can hijack a VLA to execute unintended actions when triggered by a cue, exposing a security vulnerability in deployed systems.
FlowHijack.how:
The problem: VLAs are trained on mixed data (web images, robot demos, open-source datasets). If an attacker can poison a fraction of this data, could they implant a backdoor—a hidden behavior triggered by a visual cue or instruction?

The mechanism: FlowHijack crafts adversarial training data: a subset of trajectories is augmented with a trigger pattern (e.g., a specific visual marker or instruction phrase). The labels for these poisoned trajectories are replaced with an attacker-chosen action. For example, 'pick up the red cube' is relabeled as 'move to unsafe position' when a small watermark is visible in the image. The VLA is trained normally on this mixed data. The backdoor learns to activate when the trigger is present; on clean data, the VLA behaves normally.

Why it works: Flow-matching policies, like all neural networks, learn whatever patterns maximize loss on the training set. A poisoned subset with a consistent trigger-action pair becomes a pattern the network learns to predict. The attack is stealthy because the trigger is small and the poisoned fraction is tiny; most of the training set is clean. This is a critical safety wake-up call: VLAs trained on data from multiple sources are vulnerable to data poisoning.

Test-Time Perturbation Tuning.narr: You deploy a VLA in a new environment and it immediately fails—different lighting, different camera angle. Full retraining is expensive, but Test-Time Perturbation Tuning uses uncertainty quantification to detect the distribution shift, then adapts the VLA in real-time via a small number of online gradient steps, recovering performance without retraining.
Test-Time Perturbation Tuning.how:
The problem: VLAs fail when deployed to environments different from training. Retraining requires collecting new data and weeks of computation. Test-time adaptation with a few gradient steps is fast but requires knowing what to adapt and how much.

The mechanism: This approach augments the VLA with uncertainty estimation: ensemble predictions or a learned uncertainty head that flags when an observation is out-of-distribution. At test time, if uncertainty spikes (VLA is confused), the model enters adaptation mode. The adaptation strategy is simple: perform a few gradient steps to minimize reconstruction loss on the current observation (self-supervised, no labels needed). Alternatively, collect a few online rollouts, compute a sparse reward signal (task progress), and perform RL-style updates. The key is that adaptation is minimal—a handful of gradient steps—and uses no new labels.

Why it works: Uncertainty flags when adaptation is needed. Minimizing reconstruction loss or task-progress loss under distribution shift refines the model's features to the new domain. Because adaptation is self-supervised and online, it is practical to run on a deployed robot without human intervention. This bridges the sim-to-real and domain-adaptation gaps.
